2A.method: At stage 2A the analyst should work in this order: (1) anchor the base year using the hardest primary source available—regulated quota, official trade data, company product revenue, or a credible third-party supply outlook—and cross-check with 2–3 independent demand indicators; if no direct source exists, use a proxy chain and calibrate to the historical CAGR. (2) Set forecast_growth_vs_history relative to history, using a default premium of +0.5 to +0.9pp for mature markets with structural tailwinds, +0.9 to +1.2pp for early-growth or technology-adoption markets, and 0.0 to +0.3pp for saturated markets. (3) Set region_split by first choosing the dominant demand type: manufacturing/industrial, healthcare/income, or a default balanced market, then adjust from all-market share averages. (4) Assign region_growth as gaps vs the global root, starting from APAC +1.0 to +2.0pp, NA -0.5 to 0.0pp, Europe -1.0 to +0.5pp, LATAM -1.0 to -2.0pp, MEA -0.5 to +1.0pp, and shifting premiums upward for infrastructure/regulatory buildout. (5) Split each region into countries using major-country anchors and a residual 'Rest of' line. (6) Assign country_growth gaps using structural tailwinds or constraints, with typical dispersion ±1.3pp. Evidence priority: primary demand/supply data > installed base > income/healthcare spend > manufacturing base > policy/regulation > analyst convention.

pitfalls: Copying regional shares from another market without adjusting for demand type (e.g., using APAC-heavy industrial split for US-centric pharma).
Over-extrapolating historical CAGR into forecast by adding a large premium without evidence; typical premium should be ≤1.2pp unless early-growth disruption.
Treating MEA and Africa as one region when opinions/stats often separate Africa; ensure consistent region definitions before comparing shares.
Using extreme country growth gaps from outliers (Russia -5.5pp, Nigeria +7.1pp, Israel -9.2pp) as typical; most gaps are within ±1.3pp.
Anchoring base year only to one data source without cross-check; e.g., DEA quota alone could overestimate if retail share differs.
Over-relying on analyst convention '2025 latest year' without re-basing when historical data are poor or the market has a structural break.
Setting country splits without a residual 'Rest of' for fragmented regions, causing spurious precision and overstating small-country shares.

2B.method: At stage 2B, first decide use_case_split: anchor the largest use case in the most stable structural or regulatory driver (installed base, dominant industry, mandatory use), then set the next 2-4 use cases by volume or value, and leave an 'Other' tail. Next set use_case_growth: take the market root CAGR and add segment growth premiums; premiums should be share-weighted to zero, with most absolute deviations around 0.7-1.2pp and top-to-bottom spread around 2.5-4.5pp. Finally adjust use_case_mix_by_region: start from the global use-case split, then shift regional mixes only where structural industry mix, policy, or channel evidence is strong; keep unexplained or balancing shifts at ±1-3pp. Look for regulation, installed base, infrastructure capex, and channel shift as primary evidence before relying on broad categories like 'population' or 'GDP'.

heuristics.why: Installed base and regulatory mandates concentrate demand. Across past segmented markets, seg.top_share averages 52.7%, and anchored examples include coastal desalination 76.3%, general/multispecialty hospitals 72.3%, electric utilities 59.2%, and pharmaceutical companies 56.0%. These are not uniformly distributed.

heuristics.condition: The market spans diverse consumer, industrial, or application segments with no single regulatory or installed-base anchor.

heuristics.condition: A region has a structural industry advantage in a use case, such as APAC electronics/industrial, North America healthcare/defense, Latin America agriculture, or Europe environmental monitoring.
heuristics.action: Shift that region's share of the structural use case +2 to +8pp vs global; offset with negative shifts of -1 to -5pp in less relevant use cases.

heuristics.condition: No strong local evidence, and the analyst needs to balance global shares or follow past convention.
heuristics.action: Use ±1 to 3pp shifts across regions and use cases; keep most regional changes within ±2pp, especially for large regions.
heuristics.why: Many past regional mix shifts are small and likely mechanical: Buprenorphine OUD shifts -1pp in Europe/LatAm/MEA; Technical Foam +1pp; Digital Twin DERMS +1pp. The all-market seg.country_mix_sd is about 0.9pp, so small deviations are typical.
heuristics.caveat: Do not invent causal stories for every ±1pp; report them as balancing or low-confidence adjustments.

heuristics.condition: The analyst is setting growth premiums for a full set of use cases.
heuristics.action: Ensure the share-weighted sum of premiums equals zero; target typical absolute deviation of 0.7-1.2pp and top-to-bottom spread of 2.5-4.5pp. If all premiums are positive, subtract the weighted average from every premium.
heuristics.why: Past markets show seg.cagr_dev around 0.77pp and seg.cagr_spread around 2.75pp, meaning most premiums should be modest. North America Electronic Design Services gave all vertical premiums +7 to +12pp, which is mechanically wrong because it implies every segment grows above the root.

heuristics.condition: A region is small in global market size, but the use-case shift within that region is large in percentage-point terms.
heuristics.action: Before judging global impact, multiply the regional shift by the region share. Typical region shares are NA 35.8%, Europe 27.0%, APAC 23.0%, LatAm 6.0%, MEA 5.8%.
heuristics.why: A +15pp shift in Kuwait or Qatar contributes less than 1pp to the global mix if the region is only a few percent of the world market. Past examples like Kuwait water +17pp or Qatar aquaculture +9pp should be interpreted within the Middle East Agriculture market, not as global shifts.
heuristics.caveat: If the market is defined only for that region, such as a Latin America bone cement market or Saudi kitchen market, this global weighting does not apply.

pitfalls: Avoid copying mechanical 'top share = 50%' splits; use installed-base or regulatory anchors when available.
Do not set all use-case growth premiums positive; they must be share-weighted to zero and mostly within ±2.5pp.
Do not over-interpret small ±1pp regional mix shifts; many are balancing conventions, not real demand signals.
Do not apply large GCC-style policy shifts to large diversified economies.
Do not confuse a high growth premium with a large current share; emerging segments should often remain small.
Do not ignore region size: a +10pp shift in LatAm (~6% global) is smaller than a +2pp shift in NA (~36%) for global mix.
Be skeptical of analyses where every segment grows above the root, such as NA Electronic Design Services, and normalize before using.

2C.method: At stage 2C, form opinions in this order: (1) identify the primary type dimensions—product type, technology, service model, deployment, grade—and classify what is the default/standard vs the emerging/premium type; (2) set global type_split shares for 2025 using installed base and standard-of-care, not equal splits or forced 50% anchors; (3) set type_growth premiums for each type relative to the market root using technology adoption, regulation/sustainability, brand vs generic, services/software shift, and convenience/channel shift; (4) for the most important parent types, set sub_segment_split shares and growth using application pain-points and maturity; (5) adjust type_mix_by_region only where regional maturity, industrial base, or cost sensitivity differ, keeping shifts zero-sum; (6) set price_by_region indices using income, premium mix, and commodity vs specialty. Evidence to look for first: installed base and standard-of-care, technology adoption curve stage, regulatory/policy direction, regional end-use/industrial composition, and payer/consumer preferences. Do not copy common flat-region or 50%-top-share anchors without checking them.

heuristics.condition: A market has a clear default/standard product type or technology used by most buyers
heuristics.action: Set the default type's share at 50-65% if there are 2-4 types, or 30-50% if there are 5+ types; set the rest by application niche and price tier.
heuristics.why: Past estimates cluster top type share around 50-58% (all seg.top_share mean 52.7%, n=58). Markets with established standards such as gas analyzers 58%, traditional round pizza 52%, and PU foam 45% show concentration. This is a robust house anchor but must be adjusted by installed base and standard-of-care.
heuristics.caveat: Do not apply to multi-technology markets with no standard or to premium niches like beam-combined lasers (26%) or fiber lasers (35%).

heuristics.condition: One type is legacy/installed-base and another is new/premium but small
heuristics.action: Set legacy share 50-80% and emerging share 5-20%; do not give emerging equal share yet.
heuristics.why: Current revenue follows installed base: fixed kiosks 87%, barcode scanning 86%, PMMA cement 94%, solvent-based decaf 64%, MCUs 46%. Emerging technologies remain small until replacement or regulatory drivers mature.

heuristics.caveat: If market is already past early adoption (e.g., cloud in head-end at 42%), emerging share can exceed 30%.

heuristics.condition: A type benefits from adoption of new technology or performance shift
heuristics.action: Set growth premium +1 to +4 pp vs root for the emerging/performing type; set mature legacy type -0.5 to -2 pp. If emerging type is <5% share, use +3 to +6 pp but cap extremes.
heuristics.why: Typical segment growth spread is 2.75pp (all seg.cagr_spread, n=58). Examples: hyperspectral imaging +2.9, cybersecurity services +1.9, cloud deployment +3.0, AI coaching +2.7, fiber lasers +1.7. Legacy types fall below root.

heuristics.condition: Regulation or sustainability shifts demand toward compliant types
heuristics.action: Give compliant/sustainable type +0.5 to +1.5 pp growth premium; non-compliant/solvent/legacy type -0.5 to -1.5 pp. For strong policy penalties, sustainable type can be +2 to +3 pp.

heuristics.caveat: If the new channel remains niche or requires expensive hardware, growth premium may be lower or negative.

heuristics.condition: Regions differ in adoption maturity or infrastructure stage
heuristics.action: Shift advanced/premium type share up +2 to +5 pp in early-adopter/developed regions; shift basic/build-out type share up +2 to +5 pp in emerging/late-adopter regions. Counter-shift other regions, keeping zero-sum.
heuristics.why: Head-end system: APAC hardware +3, MEA +5, NA software +2; spectral sensor: LatAm multispectral +5, MEA +2; digital twin: MEA/LatAm asset +1. Adoption curves drive mix by installed base.
heuristics.caveat: Do not use if regions have similar maturity; then shifts should be small or zero.

heuristics.condition: Regional industrial base or regulatory regime differs
heuristics.action: Set type share shift ±1 to ±3 pp in specific regions, offset elsewhere. Use +2/-2 for strong industrial or regulatory differences; +1/-1 for mild differences.
heuristics.why: Technical foam: Europe PU +3, NA high-performance +1; process analyzer: Europe gas +1, MEA +1; azelaic acid: NA pharma +2, Europe cosmetic +1. Regional end-use/regulatory orientation drives product mix.
markets: North America & Europe Azelaic Acid Market
heuristics.caveat: Do not set arbitrary non-zero shifts; they should be tied to a concrete end-use/regulatory difference.

heuristics.condition: Emerging/cost-sensitive regions have weaker infrastructure or payer budgets
heuristics.action: Shift basic/cost-effective type share up +1 to +3 pp in emerging regions; shift premium type up +1 to +3 pp in developed regions, offset zero-sum.
heuristics.why: Gel ice pack: disposable +2 LatAm, +1 MEA; collagen membrane: non-crosslinked +2 Ecuador/El Salvador, Brazil -1 toward cost. Income and infrastructure drive mix.
heuristics.caveat: Not all emerging regions use basic types; APAC often adopts premium/reusable quickly.

heuristics.condition: A parent segment contains multiple applications/technologies
heuristics.action: Set largest subsegment to 25-60% of parent if multiple; set fastest subsegment growth +1 to +3 pp vs parent, slowest legacy -1 to -3 pp. Use installed base for share, adoption for growth.
heuristics.why: Process analyzer gas subsegments: industrial gases 24%, emission 18%, hydrogen +3.0 vs industrial gases -1.5. High energy laser: counter-UAS 32%, +2.6 vs guidance -2.2. Sub-segment typical deviation is 0.88pp (all seg.sub_cagr_dev) but ranges to ±3pp.
heuristics.caveat: If subsegments are very fragmented, largest can be <25% and growth may vary outside ±3pp.

heuristics.condition: A subsegment is small (<10% share) and emerging, or mature and commodity
heuristics.action: Set small emerging subsegment growth +2 to +5 pp vs parent; mature/commodity subsegment -0.5 to -2 pp. Set larger mature subsegments near parent growth.
heuristics.why: Hydrogen in gas analyzers 9% +3.0, biomethane 5% +2.1; CV/AI 10.7% +5.7 in retail scanning; gummies 1.5% +4.0; traditional industrial gases -1.5.
markets: Global Retail Self Scanning Solutions Market
heuristics.caveat: Cap small-base extremes; do not let tiny segments distort market growth.

heuristics.condition: Product is premium/technology-intensive and regions differ in income/purchasing power
heuristics.action: Set North America/Europe price index 1.0-1.25, Asia Pacific/Latin America 0.75-0.95, MEA 0.9-1.1 (global=1.0). Use higher NA premium for specialty/consumer products.
heuristics.why: Decaf coffee: NA 1.25, Europe 1.04, APAC 0.75; UCO: NA 1.15, Africa 0.72; process analyzer: NA 1.05, APAC 0.95. Income, premium mix, and logistics produce these ranges.
markets: Global Used Cooking Oil Collection Market
heuristics.caveat: If product is undifferentiated, use parity range in 2C-14.

heuristics.condition: Product is commodity/logistics-heavy with low differentiation
heuristics.action: Set regional price indices close to 1.0 (±0.03); remote/import-dependent regions +0.05 to +0.15; low-income regions 0.95-1.00 if no premium mix.
heuristics.why: Bone cement: Brazil 1.01, Argentina 1.01, Colombia 0.99; collagen membranes: Brazil 1.02, El Salvador 0.96; India SWRO: Northeast 1.13 vs South 0.99. Small deviations reflect logistics, duties, local competition.
markets: India Seawater Reverse Osmosis (SWRO) & High-Rejection Industrial RO Membrane Market
heuristics.caveat: Even commodity products can have large regional gaps if raw material/logistics or policy demand differ.

heuristics.condition: No clear regional driver is identified for type mix
heuristics.action: Set regional type-mix shifts to zero (flat); this is a house convention to avoid spurious differences only after checking installed base, industrial mix, and regulatory regimes.
heuristics.why: Retail self-scanning held product-type mix flat across regions because the analyst saw no material difference; many past analysts also default to zero. This is acceptable when markets are homogeneous, but it is often overused.
markets: Global Retail Self Scanning Solutions Market
heuristics.caveat: Do not apply zero mechanically; if any region has different maturity, income, or industrial base, use 2C-8/2C-10.

pitfalls: Mechanical zero regional type shifts: many past analysts set type_mix_by_region flat without evidence (e.g., product type in retail self-scanning); only use zero if regional markets are truly homogeneous.
Overusing extreme growth premiums for near-zero bases: Phase 3 drugs +42.7pp is an analyst artifact, not a market lever; cap small-base premiums to +3 to +6pp unless explicitly renormalizing.
Setting every type growth to root: past opinion lists often include many ±0pp or tiny shifts; use the segment spread mean 2.75pp to ensure meaningful differentiation.
Ignoring brand vs generic when setting type_growth: branded/premium types usually deserve +0.3 to +0.6pp and generic/commodity -0.2 to -1.0pp; flat brand/generic growth is unrealistic.
Forcing 50-60% top share: in fragmented/technology-transition markets top share can be 25-40% (fiber lasers 35%, beam combined 26%); do not anchor all type splits to 50%.
Applying developed-market price premiums to commodity products: bone cement and collagen membrane should be near parity; only premium, income-sensitive products get NA/EU 1.15-1.25.
Neglecting regional zero-sum when shifting type_mix_by_region: every positive shift must be offset across regions to maintain global share.

calibration.note: Market-specific evidence (installed base, OEM/shipment data, trade data, company revenues) overrides every house default band. A house_convention band is the weakest input: use it only when nothing specific is known, and say so.
calibration.source: mimic test 2026-11-10: held-out Glass Packaging (CAL-2) and the gearbox (CAL-3, so the gearbox is not fully blind on this point) showed heuristics applied outside their conditions

calibration.note: For aftermarket, service, spare-part, repair or consumable markets, the base-year split follows the INSTALLED BASE where the assets already are (cumulative past installations and their age) - not where new capacity or manufacturing is growing today. Fast new-build regions earn a growth premium, not an inflated base-year share. Choose the heuristic whose CONDITION matches the market's demand mechanism before applying its numbers.
calibration.source: mimic test 2026-11-10: held-out Glass Packaging (CAL-2) and the gearbox (CAL-3, so the gearbox is not fully blind on this point) showed heuristics applied outside their conditions

disabled_decisions.region_split: mimic test 2026-11-10: with the region-share bands the analyst's base-year geography shares got worse on held-out markets (2.86 -> 3.94 pp; calibrated 3.66 pp) and on the gearbox (3.19 -> 7.00 pp), while every other decision improved; region shares are left to market evidence (OEM installed base), growth gaps keep their heuristics
